summary: An 1882 iron tower on a rock off De Tour Village, Michigan; removed in 1988 to a Coast Guard station at Sault Ste. Marie, where it still stands.

lens.note: Sixth-order Fresnel per the USLHS record; LighthouseFriends names the maker. Later history of the lens not in the sources read.

structures.note: 18 ft (5.5 m) per Terry Pepper and LighthouseFriends; USLHS gives 15 ft from base to lantern centre. Now at USCG Station Sault Ste. Marie, 337 Water Street.

access.note: Directory and LighthouseFriends: grounds open, tower closed. The USLHS record says 'Open to Public: No', which disagrees. The tower stands on Coast Guard property.

events.note: Congress appropriated $2,000 for a beacon light on the island (3 March 1879).
Iron tower built on the island; work finished late September 1882.
First shown the evening of 1 October 1882 as a fixed red light of 160 candlepower.
Oil storage building, 8 by 12 feet, put up in July 1884 with a bunk, which LighthouseFriends says was for nights when the keeper had to stay on the island.
Wooden oil house, ten by twelve feet, built.
Tower repainted from brown to white (report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1894); landing crib and pier built.
Lighthouse Board asked for $4,000 for a keeper's dwelling. Whether a dwelling was built is disputed: LighthouseFriends says a seven-room house was finished in 1902; Terry Pepper could not confirm it.
Keeper Abear rescued two men from the disabled motorboat J.E.O. (22 December 1916).
Keeper Abear supplied food to nine people on the tug Rambler, trapped in ice near the light, and took them and the mail to De Tour Village (27 December 1916, derived from 'five days later').
Changes to nonattended acetylene proposed in the fiscal 1920 report; work completed in fiscal 1921.
Fixed red changed to a red flash every two seconds on 9 April 1921 (LighthouseFriends only).
Frying Pan Island Dock light established atop a coal elevator, 700 feet south of the tower.
Electric siren fog signal established on the island.
Coast Guard removed the tower from the island on 8 August 1988 and took it to its Sault Ste. Marie base, where it was restored and fitted with new windows.

corrections.proposed: 1988 relocated: tower removed from the island and taken to the USCG base at Sault Ste. Marie
corrections.why: The light went out of use in 1937 (LighthouseFriends; the Michigan directory says 'Inactive since 1937'). The 1988 event is the tower's removal, not the light's discontinuance. The 1937 deactivation is already in the record.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record has 1937 (Rowlett directory) and 1988 (USLHS 'Year Discontinued'). LighthouseFriends and the directory agree the light was discontinued around 1937. The 1988 date is when the Coast Guard removed the tower, so both dates stand for different events.

The record's 4.6 m matches the USLHS 15 ft from base to lantern centre. Terry Pepper, LighthouseFriends and the Michigan directory give 18 ft (5.5 m) overall. Both figures may be right for different measurements; the story gives the 18 ft figure as the sources state it.

notes_for_editor: (1) Two station records describe this light. us-mi-frying-pan-island is the relocated tower at the Sault Ste. Marie Coast Guard station. us-mi-frying-pan-island-2 is the island site (inactive, position approximate, 45.98611, -83.89778 from the USLHS record). The story covers both. An editor may want to merge them or give the island its own entry. (2) The keeper roster is the USLHS place record for the relocated tower (slug frying-pan-island-relocated-coast-guard-station-sault-st-marie, nid 8506). roster.py did not match it by position and needed the explicit --place slug; its --json person slugs are the ones on the keeper lines. (3) The Commissioner's fiscal 1917 table of service (scan p. 270, printed p. 59) places 'N. Abear, keeper' against the Birch Point Range Lights, and the Frying Pan Island line reads 'do'. The OCR columns cannot be aligned with confidence, so the story does not use the table for Abear or for the tug Rambler. Check the page image before using it. (4) The 1891 newspaper's surname is garbled in OCR ('Joeph Rt ill'); the roster gives Joseph Riell. (5) The Light-House Board's reports for 1879 to 1890 are not in the local corpus. The 1882 construction account rests on Terry Pepper, who cites the Board's reports, and on LighthouseFriends. Those reports need checking before any 1879-1882 detail is treated as settled. The 1902 Board report is known only through LighthouseFriends' quotation. (6) Year check: the 1894 'color of the tower' entry is on printed p. 171 of the report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1894 (running head 1894, OCR head read directly). The Detour Range passage (scan p. 420, annualreportlig02statgoog) falls in the report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1897, not 1896: its running head reads 1897 and that report begins at scan p. 257. (7) LighthouseFriends' account of the name (Captain Thorn) and of Joseph Riel's relation to Louis Riel are unsourced there and not confirmed here; the story attributes both to LighthouseFriends. (8) The 1921 characteristic change (red flash every two seconds on 9 April 1921), the 1935 dock light and the 1953 siren come from LighthouseFriends only. (9) The USCG Historian's Frying Pan Island Light page could not be read (archived copy returned HTTP 403), so it is not cited. (10) Disagreements left open: the land deed (LighthouseFriends, 4 January 1881) against clear title not until 1882 (Terry Pepper); the tower's material (wrought and cast iron, Terry Pepper; steel plates, LighthouseFriends; steel, USLHS); the tower's height (18 ft overall per Terry Pepper, LighthouseFriends and the directory; 15 ft from base to lantern per USLHS); the 1902 dwelling (finished 1902 per LighthouseFriends; not confirmed per Terry Pepper); the grounds (open per LighthouseFriends and the directory; 'Open to Public: No' per USLHS). (11) Access level set to unknown, since the sources conflict. The record's own access note already carries the USLHS wording.
